title: After a rejection
objectives: Use feedback, reapplication waits and off-cycle roles after a rejection.

screens.title: Three rejections
screens.prose: Three candidates were rejected, each after a different stage. Each wants to ask why.

byKey.r0: An automated rejection after a test rarely has a person behind it to reply.
byKey.r1: Possible, but a team inbox usually sends a template. After a final, a named recruiter knows your day.

explain.text: After a final round, a named recruiter holds notes from several interviewers. That is where feedback exists, and someone can pass it on. After an automated test there is usually only a score, if that.

Notes and request, then the skill, then the plan. Leave out the argument.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The plan needs the skill, and the skill needs the evidence.

screens.prose: Nadia was rejected after a final round of four interviews. She writes to her recruiter.
screens.question: Which feedback request is best?

options.text: "Thank you for the day. Is there one area you would advise me to work on?"
"I think round 2 went better than you thought. Could you look again?"
options.why: You argued with the decision. It will not be reopened.

options.text: "Could you send each interviewer's notes and my ranking?"
options.why: You asked for too much. Firms rarely share notes or rankings; one area is answerable.

options.text: "I'm devastated. I really needed this. Please tell me what I did wrong."
options.why: You leaned on feelings. It makes a reply harder to write.

hints.text: Which email is easiest to answer in two lines?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the request a busy recruiter can answer quickly.

explain.text: One short, thankful line with one specific question is easy to answer. Arguments and long lists are not. Send it once; if no reply comes, use your own notes.

screens.prose: Waits differ. One trading firm's official rule: no retake of its test within 8 months (l4, read October 2026). Another's official posting says reapply when the next season opens (October 2026). Most firms publish no rule; candidates report about 12 months (forums, 2022 to 2026).
screens.question: How many months from a rejection in November 2026 to July 2027, when summer 2028 postings open?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count December as 1 and stop at July.

byKey.seven: You stopped at June. July is the eighth month after November.
byKey.nine: You counted November itself. Start at December.

explain.text: November to July is 8 months, the same as the official 8-month rule. So the next cycle is the natural retry at most firms. Check each firm's page: a 12-month wait would land in November 2027, late in the window.

screens.prose: Meanwhile, other routes stay open. A bank and an asset manager list official 2027 off-cycle roles in London (read October 2026). They run 3 to 6 months.

rows: Banks, funds and trading firms recruit separately

screens.question: Select all that apply: which are real routes in the meantime?

options.text: An off-cycle internship, if your course allows the time
The same role at another firm type
A programme you are still eligible for
The same firm and role again, next week
options.why: You resent at once. Most firms keep a wait, and nothing has changed yet.

options.text: Stop applying until the next cycle
options.why: You stopped. Other firms judge you fresh.

hints.text: Row 4 is the same application again.
Off-cycle, another firm type, a programme you qualify for.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the routes where you are judged fresh.

explain.text: Off-cycle roles, other firm types and programmes you still qualify for all judge you fresh. The same firm usually wants a gap and a changed application. Off-cycle roles suit a year out or a Master's, so check your course allows it.

explain.text: Each failed round points at one skill, and each skill at one course. The plan then gets dates: finish the course before the next window opens. Research Interviews and Coding Interviews come later in the course list.

screens.prose: Ella was rejected by a trading firm after its online test. Two ideas tempt her.

rows: Send the same CV to the same firm next week
Decide quant is not for her and stop
Find the skill the test exposed; train it before the next window

screens.question: What should she do?

options.text: C: find the skill and train it
A: resend the same CV next week
B: decide quant is not for her
options.why: You read one rejection as a verdict.

options.text: Apply to every firm she can find, today
options.why: You spread the same weakness wider. It fails everywhere it goes.

hints.text: What changed between the rejection and next week?
C: the skill, then the next window.

feedback.correct: Find the skill and train it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what would change the next result.

byKey.a: You resent the same CV next week. Nothing has changed, and the firm's wait rule may block it.
byKey.b: You read one rejection as a verdict on the whole path. One firm's no changes another's chance only if the same weakness is behind it (l5).
byKey.more: You sent the same application everywhere. A shared weakness fails at every firm, as l5 warned.

explain.text: In l5 we saw applications are not independent: a shared weakness fails everywhere. So the fix is to find and train it, which raises the chance at every firm at once. One rejection is information, not a verdict.

screens.prose: An edge case. Ella was rejected by a market maker after its test. A hedge fund shares its name (l2, as reported 2026).

rows: The hedge fund with the same name

screens.question: Can she apply to the hedge fund this cycle?

options.text: Yes: they are separate firms with separate applications
No: the rejection covers both
options.why: You treated two firms as one. The name is shared; the employers are not.

options.text: Only after the market maker's wait
options.why: You applied one firm's wait to another firm.

options.text: Only for the same trading role
options.why: You tied the roles together. She picks the role at the fund that fits her.

hints.text: Are these one employer or two?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether the two are one employer.

explain.text: Two firms that share a name are separate employers with separate applications (l2). The rejection and any wait apply to the firm that made them. She judges the fund's role on its own fit.

screens.prose: Why train the skill? Take $n$ independent applications, each with chance $p$. Then $$P(\text{no offer}) = (1 - p)^n$$ Fixing a shared weakness raises $p$ for every application at once.
screens.question: With $n = 20$ and $p = 0.05$, what is $P(\text{no offer})$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply 0.95 by itself 20 times.

byKey.sub: You took 20 × 0.05 from 1. Chances multiply; they do not subtract.
byKey.one: You gave one application's chance of failing. There are twenty.
byKey.any: That is the chance of at least one offer. The question asks for none.

explain.text: $0.95^{20} \approx 0.358$, against $0.12$ at $p = 0.10$. Doubling $p$ cuts the chance of no offer by about two thirds. Real applications share weaknesses, so these figures are optimistic, as l5 warned.

screens.prose: **Follow-up.** Nadia's recruiter replies to her feedback request. Pace: reply within two days.

lines: Recruiter: Thanks for asking. Your market-making round was below the bar; the others were fine.

screens.question: What should Nadia do?

options.text: Thank them, and put Market-Making Games in her plan, with dates
Ask which interviewer marked it, to explain herself
options.why: You asked to argue the round. The decision will not be reopened.

options.text: Ask for a full written report on every round
options.why: You asked again for more. One clear answer is usually the most you will get.

options.text: Do nothing; the other rounds were fine
options.why: You ignored the one signal you have.

hints.text: What has the recruiter given her?
Thank them, then train that skill.

feedback.correct: Thank them, then train the skill.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the one clear signal.

explain.text: One clear line of feedback is valuable: it names the skill. Thanking the recruiter keeps the door open for the next cycle. Then the plan gets a course and a date.

screens.prose: Your next 30 days after a final-round rejection on 1 December 2026. Put the dated steps in order. Leave out the one that does not belong.
screens.question: Order the steps. Leave out the one that does not belong.

lines.text: 1 Dec: write down every question from the day
2 Dec: send one short feedback request
8 Dec: name the skill that failed, from notes and feedback
9 Dec: start the course that trains it, three sessions a week
31 Dec: check progress and update the target list
2 Dec: apply to 40 more firms with the same CV
lines.why: You kept the 40 applications. The same CV carries the same weakness to every firm.

hints.text: Follow the dates, then ask which step repeats the weakness.
The same CV to 40 firms changes nothing.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the dates, and drop the step that spreads the weakness.

byKey.forty: You kept "40 more firms with the same CV". It sends the same weakness everywhere at once.
byKey.left-out: You left out a step that belongs. Only the 40 applications go.

explain.text: The dates make the cycle real: notes the same day, one request, then a skill and a course. Forty copies of the same CV spread the same weakness. Homework 3 asks for a failure story, and this could become yours.

ideas: Ask once for feedback, briefly, and write down every question the same day.
Waits vary: one firm's official rule is 8 months and most publish none. The next cycle is the natural retry.
Find the skill that failed and train it: that raises your chance at every firm at once.

formula.name: Raise p, not only n
formula.note: Twenty applications: 0.36 at p = 0.05, 0.12 at p = 0.10.

summary.trap: Resending the same CV next week, or reading one rejection as a verdict on the whole path.

quiz.question: Which feedback request is best after a final round?

options.text: "Thank you for the day. Is there one area I should work on?"
"Please send my scores for every round."
options.why: You asked for scores. Firms rarely share them.

options.text: "Could you reconsider? I think I did well."
options.why: You asked them to reopen the decision.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the request that is easy to answer.

explain.text: A short, thankful request with one question gets the most replies. Scores and appeals rarely do.

quiz.question: You are rejected in October 2026. How many months until summer 2028 postings open in July 2027?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count November as 1.

byKey.eight: You stopped at June. July is the ninth month after October.

explain.text: November is 1 and July is 9. As a check, a November rejection gave 8, one month fewer.

quiz.question: An off-cycle internship best suits which student?

options.text: A student on a year out, with months free outside the summer
A student with exams every term
options.why: You picked a student with no free months. Off-cycle roles run 3 to 6 months in term time.

options.text: A first-year looking for a one-week taster
options.why: You picked a taster. That is an insight week or spring week, not 3 to 6 months.

feedback.correct: A student with months free outside the summer.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Off-cycle roles run 3 to 6 months outside the summer.

explain.text: Off-cycle internships run 3 to 6 months outside the summer. They suit a year out, a Master's gap or a recent graduate.

quiz.question: Select all that apply: what can a rejection teach you?

options.text: The stage you reached
The questions you could not answer
The recruiter's feedback, if any
That you are not cut out for quant
options.why: You read a verdict into one result. One firm's no is information, not a ruling.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the information; drop the verdict.

explain.text: A rejection tells you where you stopped and what you could not answer. It says nothing final about you.
